tidbits.text: Document 13's own timeline shows the 1705 law wasn't a first move — it was the last step in a process that started with John Punch's 1640 sentence and hardened further after Bacon's Rebellion in 1676, when the colony's elite watched poor whites and enslaved people rebel together.

tidbits.text: The Threads card's own three-move answer for "Is There One America?" questions: name the promise or the principle at stake, show how it was undermined, show how it was partially redeemed (or note that it wasn't, yet). That's the shape a strong answer takes, on any document set, all year.

exemplars.text: By the early 1700s, Virginia had passed laws making slavery lifelong and hereditary, which explains why the 1705 code called enslaved people real property.

By the early 1700s, Virginia's colonial assembly had spent decades hardening the legal line between servant and slave — from John Punch's 1640 sentence, through the alliance Bacon's Rebellion showed was possible in 1676, to the 1705 slave codes that stripped enslaved people of any legal standing as people at all — which is why this law reads less like a single decision than the last step in a built system.
exemplars.what_changed: The 4 names the moment. The 5 reaches back — it names two earlier moments (1640, 1676) that explain how the colony got to 1705, so the claim is about a built system, not a single law.

techniques.name: Reach-back
techniques.explanation: Instead of describing only the document in front of you, name one earlier moment that explains how it got here. It shows you understand a process, not just a date.

techniques.name: Naming the system, not just the event
techniques.explanation: A 5 often swaps "this law did X" for "this was the last step in a system that did X, then Y, then Z." Same facts, a higher-level claim.

try_it.prompt: The 1705 law you just read defined enslaved people as property under the law, not people. Where do you still see a live argument today over who fully counts as a person, or a full citizen, under the law?
